analysis.one_liner: Restores government control of airline fares and routes and adds new passenger protections and safety rules.
analysis.headline: The Airline Reregulation Act of 1989 never got a hearing or vote in the Senate Commerce Committee, where it was referred on the day it was introduced, and it died when the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a new federal board with power to set airline fares and routes, ending the 1978-era policy of letting airlines set their own prices. It also would have required airlines to tell passengers how to check a flight's on-time record, set up a 24-hour toll-free consumer hotline, stop airlines from cancelling flights for cost reasons without 24-hour notice and replacement travel, and require at least one-third of advertised cheap fares to actually be sold at that price. It would have added safety rules too: no pairing rookie captains with rookie co-pilots, better crew training, infant safety seats on all planes, and stronger checks on aging aircraft.
analysis.who_benefits: Air travelers, who would have gotten government-set fares and routes, clearer fare advertising, notice and rebooking when flights are cancelled for cost reasons, a consumer hotline, and new safety requirements including infant seats and limits on pairing inexperienced pilots.

how_it_helps.text: Creates an independent Aviation Policy Board with the power to regulate the air fares and routes of US air carriers, reversing the deregulation of fares and routes that had been in place since 1978.

Requires airlines to print notice on every ticket jacket telling passengers how to check a flight's on-time performance record, and sets up a 24-hour toll-free hotline with performance information, consumer rights information, and dispute help.

Bars airlines from cancelling a flight for an economic reason unless they notify passengers at least 24 hours ahead and provide similar services, with exceptions only for safety-related issues like mechanical failure.
Requires fare ads to offer at least one-third of seats at the advertised price or disclose when fewer are available, and to disclose advance-purchase, refund, and minimum-stay restrictions.

Directs new safety rules: banning pairs of inexperienced captains and co-pilots, improving cockpit and cabin crew training, requiring infant safety seats on all aircraft, and strengthening identification and repair of aging-aircraft problems.

analysis.who_pays: US airlines, which would bear compliance costs for fare advertising, cancellation notice, safety training, infant seats, and aging-aircraft programs, and would lose the ability to set their own fares and routes. The federal government would fund the new board. Some costs could be passed to passengers through higher fares.

drawbacks.text: Reestablishing government control of fares and routes would undo the pricing freedom created by the Airline Deregulation Act of 1978, which economists broadly credit with lowering average airfares over time; fare and route regulation could raise prices and reduce the competition and new routes deregulation produced. This is the standard objection to re-regulation, though it is general policy knowledge rather than a claim from the bill's record.

The cancellation, advertising, and safety mandates impose real compliance costs on airlines, and the bill would create a new federal agency funded by congressional appropriations, adding taxpayer expense.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For passengers, the consumer-disclosure, cancellation-notice, and advertising rules offer clear, low-cost benefits that most travelers would notice directly. The safety provisions respond to real problems of the era, including aging aircraft. The far-reaching part is fare and route control by a new board: that is where honest trade-offs are largest, since the pricing freedom airlines had since 1978 is widely credited with making flying cheaper, and regulated fares could raise the cost of travel for many passengers. On balance it was a broad transfer of power from airlines to a new regulator, with benefits for travelers that would partly be offset by possible higher fares and taxpayer cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Howard Metzenbaum introduced the Airline Reregulation Act of 1989 in the Senate on November 8, 1989, joined by one cosponsor.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on November 8, 1989, and that was the last action in its history.
The bill had only two cosponsors, both Senate Democrats.
The Commerce Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: US airlines, which kept the freedom to set their own fares and routes without cancellation-notice or advertising restrictions and without the bill's new safety and training costs. Travelers got none of the bill's protections from it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a floor vote, so no roll calls show how parties would have split; its three sponsors were all Democrats, and opposition came in the form of committee inaction rather than any recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would end airlines' control over their own fares and routes, require 24-hour notice and replacement travel for economically motivated cancellations, force honest fare advertising, and impose new training, infant-seat, and aging-aircraft costs. Every major provision takes money or discretion from airlines and gives it to passengers or a regulator.
Ticket jackets would have to tell customers they could get on-time records through their travel agent, and agents would field more consumer inquiries. The effect is modest either way.
Stricter aging-aircraft certification, maintenance, and data requirements would create demand for inspection, maintenance, and engineering work while adding certification burdens.
